- agent-workflows:do-task: Does the work a claimed issue describes — writes and commits the change, or performs the
act and captures the evidence that it happened. Holds the scope the issue set, records
why in the commit message rather than only what, and ends by stating what state the work
is actually in rather than declaring it done. The write half of an issue; something else
judges whether it finished. - Use once an issue is claimed and the work should start, whatever kind it is — "implement
it", "fix it", "make the change", "go ahead", "do it". Code: "write the parser fix".
Docs: "update that README". Environment: "run the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate
the cert now", "run the migration", "restart it". Reach for it after take-issue has
claimed something, and when the user says do it on work already understood. Not for

- agent-workflows:file-issue: Turns something said in a session into a tracked issue that a cold agent can act on, and
copies the session log beside it wherever one can be had — always attempted, never a
reason to withhold the issue. Decides first whether the thing needs tracking at all,
searches for an existing issue before creating a second one, quotes the request in the
words it was made in rather than paraphrasing it, and states an acceptance test someone
else can check. Creates the portal every later step resolves back to. - Use whenever work is identified but not started, of any kind — not only code. Code:
"this is broken", "raise a bug", "we should track this", "someone should fix that".
Docs: "the README is wrong", "nobody can find how to run this", "that page is stale",
"this needs writing up". Environment: "staging is on the old version", "we should
upgrade that", "this config drifted", "we need a bigger instance". Operations: "the cert
expires next week", "someone has to rotate that key", "we need to migrate the data",
"that job needs re-running". Also the generic ones: "file an issue", "that's a separate
problem", "let's do that later", "add it to the backlog". Reach for it when a session
surfaces a second problem while working on a first, which is the case that most often
goes unrecorded, and when the thing is an act to perform rather than code to write. Not
for a question, a thing already underway, or a fix smaller than the issue describing it.

- agent-workflows:gen-readme: Writes a project's README from the code: researches current README convention on the
web, studies the repo from its ground truth rather than its existing docs, finds the key
points a newcomer needs first, draws every one of them as an SVG rendered to PNG, and
writes the file. Produces the README only — it does not open a PR, and review-readme
gates what it wrote. - Use whenever a README is about to be created or edited — before writing one from
scratch, and before changing an existing one. Covers "write the README", "generate a
README for this project", "our README is stale, redo it", "update the README", "document

- agent-workflows:land-pr: Merges an approved change request and cleans up after it: the code lands in the default

whether the change was reviewed and tested at this exact head, records that answer, and
pins the merge to that SHA so a head that moved cannot slip through. Refuses to merge
without the answer. - Use when an open change request should land — "merge it", "merge PR 30", "land it",
"ship it", "close out #27", "the PR is approved", "merge and clean up". Being told to run
this is a request to reach the human gate, never the answer to it. Not for opening a
change request, and not for work that ends in evidence rather than a diff.

branch first when they landed on the default one, gets the closure keyword right, and
stops for review. It does not merge, and it does not judge whether the work is good;
something before it did that. - Use when reviewed work is ready for a human to look at — "open a PR", "raise the merge
request", "push this up", "ship it", "put it up for review", "my commits are on main, get
them onto a branch". Reach for it after the work has been judged done, and when someone

the tasks", "this is too big", "split it", "that's really three things", "plan this

ordinary work that happens to have several steps, and not for filing a single issue.

the reader wants it run or wants the detail. Findings, what was checked, risks and
decisions are prepared and held; the reader acts on the next step or asks. Only a
blocked or failed next step brings its blocker up with it. Replaces the reply that mixes

where things stand, what is left, what broke, what is blocked — and the answer runs

- agent-workflows:review-readme: Gates a README before a person reads it, on three counts: it delivers for a newcomer,
it is true to the code, and it reads and looks right. Derives the key points from the
code and checks the README leads with them and ships a diagram for each, verifies every
command, path, env var and link against the source, and re-renders each diagram to catch
one that has drifted from what it is drawn from. Gates what gen-readme wrote, and any
README edited by hand. - Use whenever a README has just been created or edited, by this toolkit or by hand —
including an edit made without gen-readme, and an edit to a single section rather than
the whole file. Also on request: "review the README", "check the README is accurate",

- agent-workflows:review-work: Judges what state finished work is actually in, and routes it there. Checks the
acceptance line against the work rather than against the claim about it, sweeps what the
change left behind, and sends the result onward, back for more, back to the issue, or up
for splitting. Only one of its five outcomes reaches a change request, which is the point
of having it. - Use after work has been done and before anything ships it, every time, whatever kind it
is. Triggers: "review this", "check my work", "is this done", "did that work", "have a
look", "ready to ship?", and the end of any do-task run. Reach for it on evidence work
too, where there is no diff to read and the question is whether the act is proven. Not

- agent-workflows:reviewing-artifacts: Gates the tooling an agent reads — skills, commands, rules, CLAUDE.md — asking whether
the file has one clear job, delivers it end to end, leaves the choices the project owns
to the project, matches the repo as it actually is, and can be followed without guessing.
Returns PASS, REVISE or CUT. CUT is the verdict nothing else makes: this artifact
duplicates another or does nothing, and should be removed. - Use whenever a file an agent reads is written or changed — a SKILL.md, a slash command, a
rules file, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md — and before adding a new one to a collection, since
the overlap question is easiest to answer while it is still cheap. Also on request:
"review this skill", "is this command any good", "does this rule earn its place", "why
isn't my skill triggering", "do we need both of these". Judges whether the artifact does

- agent-workflows:reviewing-phrasing: Reviews the words of a document a person will read, and returns PASS or REVISE. Starts
by establishing what the file actually is and who reads it, because a markdown file
carries no contract the way a source file does, and the same wording is correct in a
talk track and wrong in a test case. Then runs check-prose.sh to locate the mechanical
tells by grep rather than by impression, and judges what a pattern cannot reach. - Use whenever prose a person will read is written or edited: a README, a design doc or
RFC, a test plan, a QA report, a bug report, API or CLI reference, release notes, slide
content, a demo script. Also on request: "does this read okay", "make this clearer",
"tighten this up", "write this up", "too wordy". Reach for it on a document that is
factually correct and still hard to read, and on any document an agent generated, which
is the case that most needs it and least asks for it.

- agent-workflows:reviewing-typography: Reviews how a human-read document looks — a README, prose and tables in docs/, an HTML
page — and returns PASS or REVISE. Works the way a UI designer does: group the content,
space the groups so the inner gap is smaller than the outer one, emphasize by dimming
what is not the point rather than shouting what is, hold the level count low, and judge
the page whole rather than section by section. Judges the look; the words are a separate
review. - Use whenever a document a person will read is written or restructured — a README, a
guide, release notes, an HTML page — and before it reaches its reader. Also on request:
"does this read okay", "make this scannable", "why does this look like a wall", "clean
up the formatting", "too many headings". Reach for it on a doc that is factually right
and still hard to get through, which is the case nobody thinks to ask about.

- agent-workflows:take-issue: Picks up a tracked issue of any kind and claims it: resolves which one, reads it whole

back when it cannot. Assigns it, moves the state label, cuts a branch where a diff is
coming, and stops before any work begins — so a misreading is catchable while it is still
cheap. The read half of an issue; something else does the work. - Use whenever work is about to start on something already tracked, whatever kind it is —
"work on #42", "what's next", "pick something up", "grab the next one", "I'll take that",

remember it. Not for filing something new, and not for doing the work once claimed.

1	---
2	name: review-ci-system
3	description: |
4	  Judges what a project's tests actually prove, rather than how many there are. Classifies
5	  every test by what it is allowed to touch, discards the levels that cannot answer
6	  "is this covered", and lays the rest against what the system must do — so a suite that is
7	  large, tidy and green is still reported as proving nothing when that is the truth. Writes
8	  no test and deletes none; it names the one gap worth closing and stops.
9	when_to_use: |
10	  Use whenever someone touches the machinery that tests or runs a project — creates a test
11	  file, edits one, reads one, deletes one, adds or edits a CI workflow — and whenever the
12	  question is what the tests are worth: "is this covered", "are these tests any good", "do
13	  the tests actually test anything", "the suite is green but it broke in production", "why
14	  did this ship broken", "review our test setup", "what's our coverage". Reach for it before
15	  writing a new test, because what to write is decided by what is missing, and before
16	  trusting a green suite, which is the case that never asks for review. Not for running the
17	  tests, and not for writing or deleting one.
18	argument-hint: "[path to the project, or nothing for the current repo]"
19	---
20	
21	# Review what the tests prove
22	
23	Target: $ARGUMENTS — the project under review, or this repo.
24	
25	**A test count is read as safety and is not evidence of any.** A suite can be large, evenly
26	organised, carefully commented, and green, and still prove almost nothing — because
27	everything it touches is a fake the suite wrote itself. Size, tidiness and coverage
28	percentage cannot detect that. One question can:
29	
30	> If every test passes, what is now known to work?
31	
32	That is the only question this unit asks. Everything below is machinery for answering it
33	honestly.
34	
35	## 1. Get the key points first
36	
37	**A suite cannot be judged from the tests alone.** "Counts" has no meaning until something
38	says what the system must do — so the rows come before the cells, always.
39	
40	Derive them from ground truth — the code, not the docs: entry points, build files, schema,
41	routes, config. About three, ranked, #1 the organizing idea. `analysis-sut` does exactly
42	this and is the route to prefer where it is installed; where it is not, do the study here
43	and say that is what happened. If key points were already produced in this session, reuse
44	them rather than studying twice.
45	
46	Check what came back before using it. A key point that describes structure rather than
47	naming a behaviour — *"rules are rows read once at startup"* — yields a matrix row nothing
48	can ever fill. Ask for it again as something a test could cover, and ask whether any
49	behaviour was explained only inside another point's mechanism: absorbed like that it is
50	indistinguishable from one never found, and the row will simply be missing.
51	
52	Do not derive key points from the test names. They describe what someone chose to test,
53	which is the thing under examination. Deriving the standard from the subject makes any suite
54	look complete.
55	
56	## 2. Classify every test by what it is allowed to touch
57	
58	**Never by folder. Never by name.** A directory called `integration/` full of tests that
59	mock every dependency contains no integration tests, and the name is what made that

1	---
2	name: analysis-sut
3	description: |
4	  Works out what a system must do, from its code rather than its documentation, and returns
5	  it as a short ranked list of key points — each with the paths it was derived from, the
6	  mechanism in the code's own names, and a diagram. Reads the existing docs only to report
7	  where they contradict the code. Saves nothing: the study is reproduced when needed rather
8	  than stored, because a stored one goes stale silently and is believed anyway.
9	when_to_use: |
10	  Use when the question is what a system does or what about it is worth testing — "what
11	  should we test here", "where do I start with tests", "what's worth testing", "what does
12	  this system actually do", "I'm new to this codebase", "walk me through it", "what are the
13	  moving parts". Reach for it before judging or writing any test, since what counts as
14	  coverage is decided by what must be tested, and reach for it on an unfamiliar repo before
15	  trusting anything its README says. Also called by review-ci-system, which cannot classify
16	  a suite without it. Not for finding one file or one function — that is a search.
17	argument-hint: "[path] [focus]"
18	---
19	
20	# What must be tested
21	
22	Target: $ARGUMENTS — a path and an optional focus. No path means this repo; no focus means
23	the whole system.
24	
25	**A system's documentation is a claim about it, not a description of it.** Docs are written
26	once and the code moves; nothing announces the divergence, so the stale sentence is read as
27	current and believed. One study of a well-documented repo found eleven places where its own
28	README and architecture decision records asserted things the code did not do.
29	
30	So the model is derived from the code. The docs are read afterwards, and only to report
31	where they disagree.
32	
33	## What this returns
34	
35	A ranked list, about three key points, each carrying seven things:
36	
37	| Field | What goes in it |
38	|---|---|
39	| **#** | Rank. #1 is the organizing idea |
40	| **Key point** | One line, concrete |
41	| **Ground truth** | The paths it was derived from — makes the claim checkable |
42	| **Mechanism** | What actually happens, in the code's own names: real functions, routes, tables, types |
43	| **Why it matters** | What a newcomer cannot understand without it |
44	| **Diagram** | ASCII, one per key point |
45	| **Contradicts** | Any doc claim the code does not support, or "none" |
46	
47	**Mechanism is where a study earns its keep.** *"A service talks to a database"* is not a
48	finding. *"`store.rules()` is called once at startup and zero rows throws, so the server does
49	not start"* is — it names what is there and can be checked against the file.
50	
51	## 1. Read the ground truth
52	
53	The real artifacts, in whatever form this project has them: entry points, the build or
54	package manifest, the schema, route definitions, the container or compose files, config and
55	its defaults, the top-level layout. Trace how the parts connect, not just what they are.
56	
57	Where ground truth lives varies. Those are examples, not a checklist — a Rust workspace, a
58	Terraform root and a Rails app keep it in different places, and the question is always the
59	same: what does this actually run.
60	
61	**Read the docs last.** Reading them first supplies a model, and everything after gets read
62	as confirmation of it.
63	
64	## 2. Find #1 before listing anything
65	
66	**#1 is the organizing idea: what this is, why it exists, and how its parts form one whole.**
67	For a multi-part system that is usually how the components compose and depend on each other;
68	for a single tool, the core abstraction or the main flow.
69	
70	Find it before enumerating features. A list of features assembled first will not add up to an
71	idea afterwards, and the reader gets an inventory instead of an explanation.
72	
73	Then #2 onward — the ones a diagram explains better than prose, each grounded in #1. Rank
74	them.
75	
76	## 3. About three. Four at most
77	
78	A longer list is an index, and an index is what a reader skips. Shortening is how the count
79	comes down — never by dropping a diagram from a key point that stays.
80	
81	**And never by folding one into #1.** #1 states the organizing idea and carries no other key
82	point's mechanism. A behaviour that needs its own diagram to be understood *is* a key point;
83	absorbed into #1 it keeps its words, loses its rank and its drawing, and the result cannot be
84	told apart from a behaviour never found. Where that pushes past four, demote the weakest or
85	go to five and say why.
86	
87	Prefer a behaviour to a description. *"Rules are rows read once at startup"* describes
88	structure; *"three refusals, one per stage — schema, rules, the call itself"* names something
89	a test either covers or does not. This list is what coverage is measured against, so a
90	descriptive key point yields a row nothing can ever fill.
91	
92	## 4. One ASCII diagram per key point
93	
94	Every key point gets one. #1 included: it is the organizing idea, so it is the diagram the reader
95	needs most.
96	
97	Draw the real mechanism with real names from the code. Boxes labelled *service* and
98	*database* describe every system ever built and this one not at all.
99	
100	**Count check: diagrams drawn == key points on the list.** If there are fewer, either draw the
101	rest or shorten the list.
102	
103	The count is the weaker half. Ask the other question too: **is any behaviour explained only
104	inside another key point's mechanism?** If it is, the count passes and the point is lost —
105	which is the one failure this check cannot see.
106	
107	Keep a diagram inside 80 columns. It is read in a terminal, and one that wraps is one nobody
108	reads.
109	
110	## 5. Then read the docs, and only to contradict
111	
112	With the model already derived, read the prose files — README, architecture records, example
113	config, anything under a docs directory. Report every claim the code does not support: a
114	table that does not exist, a command that would fail, a route never defined, a described
115	mechanism that was replaced.
116	
117	*Docs* here means those files. Comments inside source are read in step 1 along with the code
118	they sit in; deferring them would mean reading the same file twice.
119	
120	This pass belongs to whoever read the code, which under step 6 is the subagent. Handing it
121	back to the caller means the caller reads the docs and the code both, and the delegation
122	bought nothing.
123	
124	This costs almost nothing once the code has been read, and it is often the most valuable
125	thing returned — the contradictions are invisible to everyone who trusts the document.
126	
127	## 6. Study in the background
128	
129	Spawn one subagent for the reading and take back its whole result.
130	
131	Studying a repo means opening entry points, manifests, schemas, routes and config. All of
132	that lands in context and none of it is the answer. A subagent spends its own context and
133	returns the conclusion. Where no subagent is available, do it inline — the method does not
134	change, only the cost. One subagent, not several: step 2 requires #1 to be found before

---
name: analysis-sut
description: |
  Works out what a system must do, from its code rather than its documentation, and returns
  it as a short ranked list of key points — each with the paths it was derived from, the
  mechanism in the code's own names, and a diagram. Reads the existing docs only to report
  where they contradict the code. Saves nothing: the study is reproduced when needed rather
  than stored, because a stored one goes stale silently and is believed anyway.
when_to_use: |
  Use when the question is what a system does or what about it is worth testing — "what
  should we test here", "where do I start with tests", "what's worth testing", "what does
  this system actually do", "I'm new to this codebase", "walk me through it", "what are the
  moving parts". Reach for it before judging or writing any test, since what counts as
  coverage is decided by what must be tested, and reach for it on an unfamiliar repo before
  trusting anything its README says. Also called by review-ci-system, which cannot classify
  a suite without it. Not for finding one file or one function — that is a search.
argument-hint: "[path] [focus]"
---

# What must be tested

Target: $ARGUMENTS — a path and an optional focus. No path means this repo; no focus means
the whole system.

**A system's documentation is a claim about it, not a description of it.** Docs are written
once and the code moves; nothing announces the divergence, so the stale sentence is read as
current and believed. One study of a well-documented repo found eleven places where its own
README and architecture decision records asserted things the code did not do.

So the model is derived from the code. The docs are read afterwards, and only to report
where they disagree.

## What this returns

A ranked list, about three key points, each carrying seven things:

| Field | What goes in it |
|---|---|
| **#** | Rank. #1 is the organizing idea |
| **Key point** | One line, concrete |
| **Ground truth** | The paths it was derived from — makes the claim checkable |
| **Mechanism** | What actually happens, in the code's own names: real functions, routes, tables, types |
| **Why it matters** | What a newcomer cannot understand without it |
| **Diagram** | ASCII, one per key point |
| **Contradicts** | Any doc claim the code does not support, or "none" |

**Mechanism is where a study earns its keep.** *"A service talks to a database"* is not a
finding. *"`store.rules()` is called once at startup and zero rows throws, so the server does
not start"* is — it names what is there and can be checked against the file.

## 1. Read the ground truth

The real artifacts, in whatever form this project has them: entry points, the build or
package manifest, the schema, route definitions, the container or compose files, config and
its defaults, the top-level layout. Trace how the parts connect, not just what they are.

Where ground truth lives varies. Those are examples, not a checklist — a Rust workspace, a
Terraform root and a Rails app keep it in different places, and the question is always the
same: what does this actually run.

**Read the docs last.** Reading them first supplies a model, and everything after gets read
as confirmation of it.

## 2. Find #1 before listing anything

**#1 is the organizing idea: what this is, why it exists, and how its parts form one whole.**
For a multi-part system that is usually how the components compose and depend on each other;
for a single tool, the core abstraction or the main flow.

Find it before enumerating features. A list of features assembled first will not add up to an
idea afterwards, and the reader gets an inventory instead of an explanation.

Then #2 onward — the ones a diagram explains better than prose, each grounded in #1. Rank
them.

## 3. About three. Four at most

A longer list is an index, and an index is what a reader skips. Shortening is how the count
comes down — never by dropping a diagram from a key point that stays.

**And never by folding one into #1.** #1 states the organizing idea and carries no other key
point's mechanism. A behaviour that needs its own diagram to be understood *is* a key point;
absorbed into #1 it keeps its words, loses its rank and its drawing, and the result cannot be
told apart from a behaviour never found. Where that pushes past four, demote the weakest or
go to five and say why.

Prefer a behaviour to a description. *"Rules are rows read once at startup"* describes
structure; *"three refusals, one per stage — schema, rules, the call itself"* names something
a test either covers or does not. This list is what coverage is measured against, so a
descriptive key point yields a row nothing can ever fill.

## 4. One ASCII diagram per key point

Every key point gets one. #1 included: it is the organizing idea, so it is the diagram the reader
needs most.

Draw the real mechanism with real names from the code. Boxes labelled *service* and
*database* describe every system ever built and this one not at all.

**Count check: diagrams drawn == key points on the list.** If there are fewer, either draw the
rest or shorten the list.

The count is the weaker half. Ask the other question too: **is any behaviour explained only
inside another key point's mechanism?** If it is, the count passes and the point is lost —
which is the one failure this check cannot see.

Keep a diagram inside 80 columns. It is read in a terminal, and one that wraps is one nobody
reads.

## 5. Then read the docs, and only to contradict

With the model already derived, read the prose files — README, architecture records, example
config, anything under a docs directory. Report every claim the code does not support: a
table that does not exist, a command that would fail, a route never defined, a described
mechanism that was replaced.

*Docs* here means those files. Comments inside source are read in step 1 along with the code
they sit in; deferring them would mean reading the same file twice.

This pass belongs to whoever read the code, which under step 6 is the subagent. Handing it
back to the caller means the caller reads the docs and the code both, and the delegation
bought nothing.

This costs almost nothing once the code has been read, and it is often the most valuable
thing returned — the contradictions are invisible to everyone who trusts the document.

## 6. Study in the background

Spawn one subagent for the reading and take back its whole result.

Studying a repo means opening entry points, manifests, schemas, routes and config. All of
that lands in context and none of it is the answer. A subagent spends its own context and
returns the conclusion. Where no subagent is available, do it inline — the method does not

- the target path, absolute, and the focus if one was supplied
- steps 1 to 5, in order
- **it writes no file anywhere** (step 7), and must say so in its result
- the docs stay shut until step 5

rule nobody can report on.

## 7. It writes no file

Not in the repo, not in a scratch directory, not a cache. The list is returned in the reply
and lives in the session.

A saved study is a document, and this skill exists because documents go stale invisibly. The
study is cheap to reproduce and current every time it is reproduced; persisting it trades
that for staleness and saves nothing worth having.

Two consequences, both accepted: two sessions studying the same system each pay for it, and
there is nothing to diff against a previous study — a *what changed* would need the stored

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Ground truth read first; docs untouched until step 5
    - [ ] #1 identified before any feature was listed
    - [ ] List ranked, four key points at most
    - [ ] No behaviour explained only inside another key point's mechanism
    - [ ] One ASCII diagram per key point — count matches, each inside 80 columns
    - [ ] Mechanism written in the code's own names, not generic ones
    - [ ] Contradictions reported, or "none found"
    - [ ] Constraints handed to the subagent, and it reported which it held
    - [ ] No file written anywhere

## Report

**Two readers, two shapes.** A skill that called this one cannot answer a question, so a
payload held back from it is a payload lost:

| Who asked | What they get |
|---|---|
| A person | two lines and a question; the list held until they ask |
| Another skill, or a subagent's caller | the whole list — every field, every diagram, the contradictions — returned with no offer and nothing held |

    STUDIED — 4 key points, #1 the validation gate on the only path out.
    11 places the docs contradict the code.
    Next: review what the tests prove against these.
    Want the list?

When the code will not yield an idea, that is a verdict rather than a shorter list:

    NOT STUDIED — no entry point resolves; this looks like a library with no assembled
    system to describe.
    Next: name what runs it, and I will study that instead.

content.content:
project that is not there.
- Ollama runs offline to survey the corpus and surface candidate rules a human
  then writes. It is never in the request path.
- Node.js 18 or later, TypeScript, ESM. Fastify for HTTP, chosen because field
  structure is already constrained by a schema and Fastify validates request
  bodies against JSON Schema natively — so malformed submissions are refused
  before any rule runs, and the two produce different response shapes.
- A rule is a row in the database, added and switched off one at a time, and read
  from it once at startup and never reloaded. There is no reload endpoint, so the generating
  agent has no mechanism by which it could relax a rule that keeps rejecting it.
  This also closes the tension the README used to flag against ADR-0001, which
  says rules are "baked into the deployed image rather than read from a mounted
  path": there is no mounted path any more. What ADR-0001 protects is unchanged.
- No rule applies across all fields, and there is no inheritance between fields.
- The server holds no state between requests. What the database holds is the
  operator's configuration and the operator's reference material, both read-only
  from the server's side, so the same test case submitted twice is still answered
  identically.
- Vitest, exercising four seams: the HTTP surface with a stubbed TestLink client
  and a stubbed document store, application startup with the rules a database
  answered with, the real TestLink client over a stubbed tool caller, and the real
  store over both a stubbed query seam and an in-process Postgres. The last two
  exist because the first is deliberately stubbed — the suite must not need a live
  TestLink or a live database — which would otherwise leave the tool calls, the
  SQL, and the reading of what comes back untested. No test reaches into the
  matcher or the offset calculator directly.

## Not decided

- Deployment shape.
- Whether the database becomes the source of truth imported into production
  TestLink, or a cache in front of it. ADR-0004 left this open and ADR-0005 did
  not close it.

## Out of scope

Duplication detection, ambiguity detection, requirement traceability, and a
generation harness for test plans and test cases. Each is a separate project.

content.content:
path on the process ADR-0001 exists to keep off one, and defends the property by
network reachability rather than by the server holding an object that cannot
write. The weaker guarantee was not worth the convenience.

**Writing with SQL, out of band.** Chosen by the maintainer. ADR-0005 rejected
this on the grounds that it leaves no supported path from a written Rule Set to a
running server. That objection is answered rather than dismissed: the schema
ships in the repository as `schema.sql`, the README documents the statements that
write a Rule Set and a Reference Document, and the suite extracts and runs those
statements against an in-process Postgres, so what is documented is what is
tested. The path is supported; it is simply not automated.

ADR-0005's other objection, to seeding on first startup, is not answered because
it no longer applies: nothing seeds. The server gained no write, and "first

## #1 — A validate-then-write gate in front of TestLink, with no write path back to its own configuration

**Key point.** Every write route runs the Rules *before* it calls TestLink and returns 422 without writing; every read route runs the same Rules and never refuses; and the object holding the Rules and Reference Documents exposes no write at all, so the running system cannot relax a Rule or author the material it validates against.

**Ground truth.**
`/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/violation.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/reference-document.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/postgres-store.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/testlink-client.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/server.ts`

**Mechanism.** `buildApp({ testlink, documents, rules, logger })` takes three collaborators and defines 16 routes. On `POST /projects/:projectId/suites/:suiteId/test-cases` and `PUT /test-cases/:id`, the handler's first statement is `findViolations(request.body, bound.testCase)`; if `violations.length > 0` it `return reject(...)` — 422, `{ violations, ruleSetVersion }` — and `testlink.createTestCase` / `testlink.updateTestCase` is never reached, so a rejected Test Case is unwritten by construction rather than by rollback. `GET /test-cases/:id` and `GET /reference-documents/:id` call the same `findViolations` (against `bound.testCase` and `bound.referenceDocument`) and always answer 200 with the content and the violations as sibling keys — `versioned({ testCase, violations })` — never merged into the served Fields, never refused (`app.ts:236-240`, `app.ts:422-430`). `DELETE /test-cases/:id` and all eight `/projects` and `/suites` routes run no Rule at all; `app.ts:276-278` says why: no Rule binds to a Project or Test Suite. **Why it matters.** A newcomer looking for the "validation service" finds no validate-only endpoint and no rule-management API, and could conclude validation is advisory. ## #2 — What a Rule actually does to text: word-standing Terms, single-character Symbols, and Exceptions that suppress by span containment

**Key point.** A Term fires only where the match stands as a word (a word runs through `-` and `_`), in any casing, with the phrase's internal spacing relaxed to `\s+`; a Symbol fires on every occurrence of one character unless `flanked='whitespace'` narrows it, where the edge of the Field counts as whitespace; an Exception suppresses a match only when the match falls wholly inside a span the Exception matched, and only for the Rule it belongs to.

**Ground truth.**
`/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/violation.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/rule-set.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/default-rules.sql`

**Mechanism.** `findViolations(content, ruleSets)` iterates the `Map<field, RuleSet>` it was handed, skips any Field whose value is `undefined`, and dispatches per Rule to `termViolations` or `symbolViolations`. `matcherFor(term)` escapes regex metacharacters, rewrites `\s+` to `\s+`, and compiles with flags `giu` — so `wireless network` matches across a line break. `standsAsWord` then rejects a hit whose neighbour character matches `/[\p{L}\p{N}_-]/u`, which is why `no-utilise` leaves `utilises` and `re-utilise` alone. `symbolViolations` walks `value.indexOf(symbol, …)` and, when `rule.flanked === 'whitespace'`, requires `isGap` on both sides, where `isGap(undefined) === true`. Suppression is `suppressedSpans(value, rule.exceptions)` — the Exception is matched by the same `matcherFor` but with **no** word-standing test, so it matches inside longer words — and `isSuppressed` requires `offset >= span.start && offset + text.length <= span.end`. Each Violation carries `{ field, rule, reason, text, offset }` with `text` being the casing found, not the casing written, and no suggested replacement. `schema.sql`'s `a_symbol_is_one_character` check uses `looks_for like '_'` (one character, not one byte) and `rule-set.ts`'s `checkStoredRule` re-checks it as `[...looksFor].length !== 1`; the shipped `default-rules.sql` writes 74 Terms and 15 Symbols against all five Fields = 445 rows (verified by counting the file).

**Why it matters.** This is the entire definition of "violation" in the product — everything else is plumbing. A newcomer who assumes substring matching will mispredict every result, and an operator writing rules cannot reason about `default-rules.sql`'s 445 rows without knowing that `-` inside a word is a word character to a Term and a whitespace-flanked target to a Symbol.

**Diagram.**

   TERM                                  SYMBOL

   standsAsWord(start, text)                 isGap = /\s/ OR edge of Field

                                             |

```

## #3 — Five answer shapes, decided by pattern-matching testlink-mcp's prose, and anything unrecognised escalates as an outage

**Key point.** A caller tells apart schema refusal (400), Rejection (422), nothing-there (404), wrong prefix (409) and outage (500) by shape alone, never by reading a message — and the classification is made in one place, `McpTestLinkClient.place()`, by three narrow regexes with `throw` as the default.

**Ground truth.**
`/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/mcp-testlink-client.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/tool-caller.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/stdio-tool-caller.ts`

**Mechanism.** `app.setErrorHandler` turns any `error.validation` into `400 { refusal:'schema', message }` — carrying no `violations`, so it cannot be misread as a Rejection, and no `ruleSetVersion`, because no Rule ran. `reject()` produces `422 { violations, ruleSetVersion }`. `nothingThere()` produces `404 { message: 'TestLink holds no …' }` — no `refusal`, no violations, no version. `answer(tool, args, alsoTheCallers?)` makes exactly one tool call and reads the result three ways: `result.isError`, or `reportedProblem(content)` (TestLink puts a `code` + `message` where a result should go), then `deniedIn(content)` (`status === false` → throw). `place()` checks, in order: `reportsUnconfirmed` = `/Confirmation failed/i` → `unconfirmed` → route answers `409`; `reportsMissingTool` = `/Unknown tool/i` → throw naming `expectedTestLinkMcp = '1.6.0'`; `reportsAbsence` = `/does not exist|not found/i` → `absent` → route answers 404; **everything else throws**, so an unrecognised failure is an outage, never a "not there". Absence is read only out of what TestLink said *about the call*, never out of served content (`mcp-testlink-client.ts:205-221`). `idOf()` throws when a create answered with no id at top level or in `additionalInfo`, and treats `0` and `''` as no id — a write that "succeeded" without an id is a failure. `listProjects` and `createProject` also throw on `absent`, because nothing was named to be missing.

**Why it matters.** The whole boundary is text over stdio (`ToolResult` is `{ text, isError }` and nothing more). A newcomer will look for structured error codes and find two regexes; without knowing the default is `throw`, they cannot see that adding a fourth wording is the standing maintenance cost, nor why 404 and 500 are the two halves of the same failure.

## The project's own admissions — quoted

The gap is not inferred here. The project states it in three places, and one of them ships the infrastructure to close it.

> `docker-compose.yml:6-9` — "TestLink is: the suite runs against a stubbed one and needs nothing here. **That part is for the checks the suite cannot make — that a write lands, that the id it answers with is the id a read answers to, and that TestLink's own wording for a Test Case that is not there is the wording the client matches.**"

> `docs/adr/0006-…md:33-35` — "the suite extracts and runs those statements against an in-process Postgres, so what is documented is what is tested. **The path is supported; it is simply not automated.**"

> `test/database.test.ts:62-66` — "Applying it twice is safe by construction — every statement is `if not exists` — but that is not asserted here: **the in-process Postgres refuses to re-parse the second apply, so a test of it would be a test of pg-mem's limits** rather than of the schema."

The `docker-compose.yml` quote is the sharpest thing in this review: it names three checks the suite cannot make, and the same file provisions a real Postgres 17 and a real TestLink to make them with. The means to fill the top three rows already ships in the repository. Nothing uses it.

## The three recurring findings — all three present

**The oracle test.** `test/submit-test-case.test.ts:39-42` asserts `expect(response.json()).toEqual({ id: 'testlink-1', ruleSetVersion: response.headers['rule-set-version'] })`. `'testlink-1'` is minted by the stub the test wrote — `return { id: \`testlink-${this.written.length}\` }` — and `ruleSetVersion` is checked against the response's own header. Both halves of that assertion are the code agreeing with itself. Same shape at `test/manage-projects.test.ts:29`: `expect(response.json()).toEqual(stubProjects)`, where `stubProjects` is the module constant `StubTestLinkClient.listProjects()` returns verbatim.

**The second implementation.** `test/stub-testlink-client.ts` is 206 lines that reimplement TestLink: it mints three id namespaces (`testlink-N`, `project-N`, `suite-N`), enforces prefix confirmation with its own three-way `'deleted' | 'unconfirmed' | 'absent'` return, enforces project and suite existence, and keeps held content and written content deliberately apart. Eleven of its behaviours drive assertions. **Nothing checks it matches the real thing.** `mcp-testlink-client.test.ts` is the nearest candidate for a contract test, but it binds the *real client* to *recorded strings* — it never meets the stub, and the two are free to disagree. pg-mem is the second such implementation, standing in for Postgres 17.

**Islands.** `grep -rnE "beforeEach|afterEach|beforeAll|afterAll" test/` returns nothing. There is not one lifecycle hook in the suite. `empty()` returns a fresh pg-mem database per call; `configured()`, `running()`, `applied()` and `serving()` rebuild the world inside each test. Nothing is threaded between tests and nothing is torn down — because nothing is real enough to leak. There is also no `vi.mock` or `vi.spyOn` anywhere: every substitution is by constructor injection, which is the tidy version of this and does not change what is reached.

## Verdict

**The suite proves that this codebase agrees with three fakes written by the same author** — a hand-written TestLink, a hand-written query seam, and a JavaScript reimplementation of Postgres. It is genuinely strong within that boundary: 225 cases, no test reaching into `matcherFor` or the offset calculator directly, the schema and the README's own SQL blocks executed rather than restated, and a discipline about response shapes that most suites do not have.

**It does not prove that a write reaches TestLink, that the id a write answers with is the id a read answers to, that `schema.sql` is SQL Postgres 17 accepts, or that the three regexes in `place()` still match the wording testlink-mcp emits.** That last one is the quiet one: #3's entire five-shape contract — the difference between a 404 and a 500 — rests on `/does not exist|not found/i` matching prose from a third-party server that nothing re-checks. A wording change there turns an outage into "nothing there", silently, with all 225 still green.

And nothing runs the suite anyway. There is no CI.

**First gap worth closing:** an acceptance test through the `docker compose up` environment the repo already ships — submit one clean Test Case, then read it back by the id the write answered with, against the real TestLink. It closes two of the three checks `docker-compose.yml` names in one test, and it is the smallest change that puts a single mark above the line.
